title: Should school start later?
text:
Many children are tired in the morning. Alarm clocks ring early, buses are crowded, and lessons begin while some students are still half asleep. Should schools start later in the day? Scientists and teachers are divided, and it is worth looking at both sides.

The case for a later start

Researchers who study sleep say that children aged ten to thirteen need about nine to eleven hours of sleep each night. When they do not get enough, they find it harder to concentrate, they make more mistakes, and they can become bad-tempered. In some schools that moved the start of the day by an hour, teachers reported that students were more alert and arrived on time more often. A well-rested brain remembers more of what it is taught.

The case against

However, a later start also brings problems. Many parents begin work early and cannot drop their children off at a later time. School would also finish later in the afternoon, leaving less time for sport, clubs and homework before dark. In hot countries, afternoons can be uncomfortably warm, so lessons are better placed in the cooler morning.

What can be done?

Some experts suggest a compromise. Schools could keep the same start time but ask children to go to bed earlier, and families could switch off screens one hour before sleep. Others suggest that the hardest subjects, such as mathematics, could be timetabled for mid-morning when students have woken up properly.

In my view, no single timetable suits every school. Each community should look at its own climate, its families and its children before deciding. The most important thing is that every child gets enough sleep, because a tired mind cannot learn.
